procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Supreme Court dismissing Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 458 of 2015 in limine on January 06, 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge made a Reference to the High Court for confirmation of the death sentence imposed on the petitioner. The petitioner also challenged his conviction and sentences by filing Criminal Appeal No. 80 of 2014 before the High Court. The High Court heard the appeal and the Reference together, upheld the conviction, and confirmed the death sentence vide its judgment dated July 09/10, 2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner preferred Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 458 of 2015 against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the SLP in limine on January 06, 2015. The petitioner then filed a Review Petition (Criminal) No. 388 of 2015 seeking review of the dismissal order. The Supreme Court allowed the Review Petition, recalled the order dismissing the SLP, and restored SLP(Criminal) No. 458 of 2015 to its original number.

directions: The order dated January 06, 2015 is recalled.
SLP(Criminal) No. 458 of 2015 is restored to its original number.

issue.issue_text: Whether a review petition should be allowed against an order that dismissed a special leave petition in limine and without providing any reasons.

facts: The petitioner was convicted and given a death sentence, which was confirmed by the High Court.
The petitioner then filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment.
The Supreme Court dismissed this SLP at the preliminary stage ('in limine') with a one-word order, "Dismissed," without providing any reasons.
The petitioner filed the present petition seeking a review of that dismissal order.
law: The Supreme Court held that in cases where a death sentence has been awarded by lower courts, the Court has a duty to conduct an independent examination, 'unbound by the findings of the trial court and the High Court'.
This approach is considered a 'time-honoured practice' of the Court.
Therefore, an SLP filed in a case involving a death sentence should not be dismissed without the Court providing reasons, at least concerning the sentence itself.
application: The Court applied the legal principle to the facts of the case.
It noted that the petitioner's SLP, which challenged a death sentence, was dismissed 'in limine' with a one-word order and no supporting reasons.
The Court found that this procedure was inadequate given the gravity of a death penalty case and the Court's established practice of independently examining such sentences.
Even if the conviction itself is sound, the Court must provide a reasoned order if it intends to affirm a death sentence at the SLP stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the petitioner's SLP challenging a death sentence was dismissed in limine and without any reasons, the review petition should be allowed. The Court recalled its original order of dismissal and restored the Special Leave Petition for a fresh hearing.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a review petition should be allowed against an order that dismissed a special leave petition in limine and without providing any reasons.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's senior counsel, Mr. Naphade, argued that under Article 137 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to review its own judgments or orders.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: As a general rule, trial courts, after recording a conviction, must adjourn the matter to a future date to allow both the prosecution and the defence to present relevant material on the question of sentencing before the sentence is pronounced.
obiter: In cases involving the death sentence, it is the practice of the Supreme Court to examine the materials on record firsthand and arrive at its own conclusions on all issues of fact and law, without being bound by the findings of the trial court and the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A cumulative effect of all the circumstances does suggest that special leave petition filed in those cases where death sentence is awarded by the courts below, should not be dismissed without giving reasons, at least qua death sentence. There may be cases where at the Special Leave Petition stage itself, the Court may find that insofar as conviction is concerned there is no scope for interference at all as such a conviction for offence under Section 302 is recorded on the basis of evidence which is impeccable, trustworthy, credible and proves the guilt of the accused beyond any shadow of doubt. At the same time, if death penalty is to be affirmed even while dismissing the Special Leave Petition in limine, it should be by a reasoned order on the aspect of sentence, at least.
legal_tests_applied: Since death sentence can be awarded only in the ‘rarest of rare cases’, the Court is supposed to give ‘special reasons’ when it choses to award death sentence.

Proper exercise of sentence discretion calls for consideration of various factors like the nature of offence, circumstances—both extenuating or aggravating, the prior criminal record, if any, of the offender, the age of the offender, his background, his education, his personal life, his social adjustment, the emotional and mental condition of the offender, the prospects for the rehabilitation of the offender, the possibility of his rehabilitation in the life of community, the possibility of treatment or training of the offender, the possibility that the sentence may serve as a deterrent to crime by the offender or by others.
why_appellant_won: The court accepted that a special leave petition in a death sentence case should not be dismissed without giving reasons, at least regarding the death sentence itself.
The court reasoned that even if the conviction is sound, affirming a death penalty requires a reasoned order on the sentence.

The requirement to provide 'special reasons' for a death sentence, after considering mitigating and aggravating circumstances, is incompatible with an unreasoned dismissal of a special leave petition.

policy_considerations: When it comes to providing hearing in cases where the judicial mind is to be applied in choosing the sentence between life imprisonment and death, this requirement assumes greater importance.

In cases of death sentence, the court intends to examine the materials on record first hand, in accordance with the time-honoured practice of this Court, and come to our own conclusions on all issues of facts and law, unbound by the findings of the trial court and the High Court.
